summary: A 1974 note proposing standard file formats for sending documents across different computer environments. The aim was to let a document sent from one kind of system be read on another. Its status is unknown.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 678 proposes standard formats for document files shared across network systems. Each format specifies page dimensions and which control characters a receiving system should use when printing.

subtitle: Six proposed formats for exchanging documents that can be printed on different systems.

tldr.problem: Documents prepared and printed on different systems can be mishandled because systems make different assumptions about character codes, page size and format controls.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 678 defines six standard file formats with a shared NVT ASCII code set and specified page dimensions, control characters and overstriking rules.
tldr.outcome: The proposal lets an author identify a file's format so a recipient can process and print it with knowledge of its layout rules.

today: The unit records RFC 678's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It proposes standard file formats for documents exchanged across network systems.

sections.title: Why Documents Need Standard Formats
sections.content:
The RFC says that online documents often looked different when processed by systems and devices with different assumptions. It proposes standard file formats and describes the expected printed form, so an author can advertise a file by name and format and a recipient can understand its controls and logical page size.

These are usage descriptions between the file's originator and receiver, not new FTP data types, modes or structures. Some hosts may need programs to convert between local formats and the proposed standard formats.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared file can print differently on different systems unless they agree on its layout rules. The proposal gives authors a way to identify those rules for recipients.

sections.title: Character Set, Pages and Controls
sections.content:
The formats standardize the character set, format controls, logical page area, and how overstruck or underlined characters are represented. The proposed code set is Network Virtual Terminal (NVT) ASCII in an eight-bit byte with the high-order bit zero.

A physical page is the paper or other medium; a logical page is the text area measured in lines and characters. Each site maps the logical page onto its own printing device. Control characters such as form feed, carriage return and line feed direct page and line movement; the RFC recommends avoiding horizontal and vertical tabs in document files because they are difficult to enforce consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: The file describes a logical page, while each site decides how that page fits its printer. Shared control characters tell the printer when to move to a new line or page.

sections.title: Six Standard Format Choices
sections.content:
The proposal defines formats for basic documents, hard-copy terminals, full-width line printers, card images, centered documents and bound documents. Their page dimensions and active controls differ. For example, Format 1 has a logical page of 60 lines by 72 characters; Format 3 is 60 lines by 132 characters; Format 4 has an 80-character page width, and each card image is followed by CR-LF.

For Format 4, trailing spaces at the end of a card image need not be included in the file; an early CR-LF means the rest of the image contains spaces. Formats also specify whether overstriking is represented by line or by character, or not used.
sections.plainLanguage: The six formats cover several uses, from ordinary documents and terminals to line printers and card images. Each one states its page size and which controls are active.

sections.title: Handling Files That Overflow
sections.content:
The RFC notes that overflow can happen when the physical page is smaller than the logical page or when a file exceeds its declared format. For excess length, a processor should force a form feed when the minimum physical or logical page length is exceeded.

For excess width, the RFC suggests either discarding characters up to the next carriage return or forcing carriage-return and line-feed actions. These are implementation suggestions for programs that process files in the proposed formats.
sections.plainLanguage: If a file is too long or wide for the declared page, the receiving program needs a rule for what to do. The RFC suggests starting a new page or trimming the overlong line.
